description: Hand-written shallow/deep answer pairs for the V0 judge evaluation. Each pair shares one question and one context set (real chunk ids from the committed corpus). 'shallow' is a faithful restatement of a single chunk; 'deep' synthesises across several sources in the same context set. 'ungrounded' items are deliberately rich and specific but unsupported by their contexts — they exist to test the faithfulness cap.
author: independent evaluation agent (not the slice builder)

pairs.question: How do I make my resume ATS-friendly?
pairs.shallow: To make your resume ATS-friendly, follow the dos and don'ts. Don't use Photoshop, Canva or other graphic editors, because the ATS might struggle with complex design. Avoid colours and highlights and keep it clean and simple. Don't use tables, footers, headers, images or emojis, because all of those can confuse the ATS. Never use columns, because the ATS might read them out of order without knowing they are columns. Skip symbols. Stick to Google Docs or Word instead.
pairs.deep: Treat ATS-friendliness as two separate problems, because the sources here are describing two different filters. The first is machine parsing. The retired big-tech hiring manager is explicit that the ATS scanner is the first line of filter, and his rules all follow from one thing — the parser reads a flat document. So no Photoshop or Canva, no tables, footers, headers, images or emojis, no colours or highlights, and above all never columns, because the parser can read them out of order without knowing they are columns. He pairs this with typography that survives the same pass: Google Docs or Word, basic fonts like Arial or Times New Roman at 11–12pt, consistent margins you can shrink to half an inch, standardised date formats, and standard section headings like 'Experience' and 'Skills' so the ATS can categorise your information correctly. The second problem is keyword matching, and the three sources disagree about where the keywords come from. The hiring manager's framing is the pizza-topping one — the reader is scanning for the specific toppings they want, so you give them exactly those. The machine-learning creator makes the method concrete: you can't know the predefined list for certain, so you mine the required qualifications in the job description, which vary from listing to listing. The recruiter reviewing AI-engineer resumes shows what that list actually looks like in one market segment — AI, LLM, NLP, Python (preferred over C or Java), agentic frameworks, LangChain, MCP, A2A, RAG, TensorFlow or PyTorch, Git/GitHub, API design. Notice what the recruiter adds that neither of the others does: he says nothing counts in a standalone technical-skills section, and that a specific bullet format is what actually matters for everyone except high-level managers and job hoppers. So the two filters pull in opposite directions on one point. Keyword density argues for listing more; the ML creator warns that if you add too much, nothing stands out, and the recruiter says a skills dump scores zero. The resolution the sources jointly support is that keywords earn their place inside experience bullets in a parseable format, not in a decorative skills block.
pairs.note: shallow restates chunk :4 only; deep spans _MT4SgfQ8QY, FpW8aiJPvts and by8wrrXW3So and resolves the density tension

pairs.question: How long should my resume be, and what should I cut?
pairs.shallow: Your resume should be one page. It isn't about cramming every single skill and everything you have done onto the page — it is about showcasing the right skills for the job, so think quality over quantity. When a resume is packed with irrelevant information it does three things: it makes it harder for the hiring manager to see why you are the right fit because the extra fluff dilutes your strengths, it slows them down because it is too much reading, and it can distract them from what really matters and makes you stand out. Just because you know JavaScript, Python and Go does not mean you need to list all of them.
pairs.deep: All three creators land on one page, but each derives it from a different constraint, and reading them together tells you what to cut rather than just how much. The hiring manager's constraint is signal dilution: extra fluff makes it harder to see why you are the right fit, slows the reader down, and distracts from what makes you stand out — so knowing JavaScript, Python and Go is not a reason to list all three. The machine-learning creator's constraint is time: a recruiter spends an average of seven seconds on a resume, and big-tech companies receive hundreds if not thousands of applications a day, so one page is the budget that fits the scan. The recruiter's constraint is recency: giving equal weight to a job from 2023 and one from 2004 makes everything blur, so the last five to seven years is your proving ground and older work gets cut to two or three bullets, and only if it reinforces what you are doing now. Two of them also give you an operational test rather than a rule. The ML creator's is the 'so what' question — he cut the courses 'Deep Learning 1' and 'Automatic Image Analysis' from his own resume because neither he nor the recruiter can tell what was actually taught in them, and demonstrated the same knowledge through experience and projects instead. He extends this to the education section generally: companies hire for skills and experience, and education is at best a product of those with no real demonstration. The same logic drives his ordering advice — if your projects are more relevant than your jobs, projects go first, then experience, then selected publications, then education — and his admission that his own summary sat at the bottom, that he still got the interviews, and that he has since moved skills to the top because a recruiter who only glances will look straight for the minimum skill requirements and will never read a dull summary. Put the three constraints together and the cut list is ordered: anything failing 'so what' goes first, then anything older than about seven years that does not reinforce your current direction, then anything that is true but not relevant to this specific listing.
pairs.note: shallow restates _MT4SgfQ8QY:2; deep unifies three constraints and derives an ordered cut list

pairs.question: Should the top of my resume be a professional summary or a skills section, and what should it say?
pairs.shallow: Put the skills section directly at the top and replace the summary. Imagine the recruiter, Joe: he has to go through hundreds of same-looking, boring resumes and only takes seven seconds to glance at each one, so he will never read a dull summary section — he will look directly for the minimum requirements of skills. The creator's own skills section was at the bottom and he still got the interviews, but he has already changed it for future applications. Once Joe can see that you at least list the skills he is looking for, you then need to briefly demonstrate those skills and convince him they have some substance.
pairs.deep: The sources here actually disagree about the summary, and the disagreement is more useful than either position on its own. The machine-learning creator would delete it: the recruiter has hundreds of near-identical resumes and seven seconds each, so a dull summary is dead space and the skills section belongs at the top where the minimum requirements get checked. He concedes his own summary sat at the bottom and he still got the interviews, which tells you the placement was not what won them. The recruiter with the hiring-meeting experience keeps the summary, but for a job the ML creator never considers: risk disclosure. Her argument is that a recruiter reading two hundred resumes a day never stops to investigate something vague, so a gap, a pivot, a short stint or a strange transition gets filled in with a story you did not write. Her fix is to put the explanation at the top — time off to care for a parent goes in the summary, a three-month role gets a one-line reason in the work experience, as in 'Operations Manager, March 2022 – May 2022, position impacted by departmental reorganisation, seeking a role with long-term growth'. That is not oversharing; it is removing the mystery. Her wider frame — the manager is hiring a safe pair of hands, someone who will not make things worse — is what makes the summary load-bearing, because vagueness reads as risk rather than as modesty. The third voice, the recruiter reviewing AI-engineer resumes, cuts across both: he says nothing counts in the technical skills section, nothing at all, which undercuts the ML creator's 'skills at the top' remedy, and he insists on one specific bullet format for everyone except high-level managers and job hoppers. Taken together, the defensible reading is that the top of the page is scarce and should be spent on whatever most reduces the reader's uncertainty. If your history is clean, that is the skills the listing names; if you have a gap, a pivot or a short stint, it is the one-line explanation, because an unexplained anomaly costs you more than a missing keyword does.
pairs.note: shallow restates FpW8aiJPvts:1; deep surfaces and resolves a genuine cross-source disagreement

pairs.question: How should I write the bullet points on my resume?
pairs.shallow: The verbs you use shape how senior you look. A bad bullet is 'Worked on a migration project for internal tools' — tools for what, what do they do, what happened, what was the point? A better one is 'Led migration of internal tools to cloud, cutting infrastructure costs by 25%', because now the reader knows what you did and what you delivered. An even better version would add context about the point of the project and who it helped. Fix your verbs and your resume immediately feels stronger.
pairs.deep: Three requirements have to hold in the same sentence, and each source supplies one. The recruiter supplies the verb: the first thing a skimmer sees is the job title and the first word of every bullet, and 'helped', 'supported' or 'worked on' signals that you were a passenger even if you were running the show. 'Worked on a migration project for internal tools' fails because nothing about it is legible; 'Led migration of internal tools to cloud, cutting infrastructure costs by 25%' passes. Her wider criterion is that every bullet should make you look like someone who has already done the job — recent, relevant, clear results that say 'I have done this before and I can do it again' — because a manager is hiring a safe pair of hands and a bullet that reads as a list of random tasks with no outcomes feels risky rather than merely unimpressive. The machine-learning creator supplies the middle of the sentence: the mechanism. Saying you 'built a large custom dataset' does not say much on its own, so he names the module, the database, Python, pandas and PostgreSQL, or pairs experiment tracking with Weights & Biases, which demonstrates the skill and the framework at once. He warns this needs balance — enough technical detail to be credible, enough abstraction that the recruiter can follow. He also supplies the end of the sentence: quantify. 'Developed a model with good performance' loses to 'developed a model with an F1 score of 39', and the numbers do double duty — they make you look invested because you know the details, and many metrics are intuitive to a non-specialist. He is honest about the limit: a 95% success rate reads instantly, an F1 of 39 does not unless the reader knows the metric, so pick the number your reader can actually feel. The recruiter's last constraint is what stops all of this collapsing into one register. If every bullet leans technical you look like a builder without direction; if every one leans strategic you sound like fluff and she wonders whether you can roll up your sleeves. The best resumes balance technical credibility, business impact and leadership — 'Senior engineer, developed an internal reporting tool in Python' shows only one face, where a bullet built around a $200 million product line translated out of research shows several. So: strong leading verb, named mechanism, intuitive number, and across the page a deliberate mix of the three kinds of value.
pairs.note: shallow restates eGmZZFJ-8PY:6; deep composes a single sentence template from three sources

pairs.question: How should I handle an employment gap or a very short stint on my resume?
pairs.shallow: Your resume should briefly explain the risky stuff up front. If you took time off to care for a parent, say so in the summary. If you left a job after three months, give a one-line reason in your work experience. You do not need to overshare — you just need to make the recruiter understand what happened. A bad example is 'Operations Manager, March 2022 to May 2022' with no context and no explanation. A better one is 'Operations Manager, March 2022 to May 2022. Position impacted by departmental reorganisation, seeking a role with long-term growth.' If you have a gap, 'Career break, January 2023 to June 2023, family caregiving responsibilities, now available full-time' is simple and clear with no mystery.
pairs.deep: The instruction is to explain the anomaly on the page, and the reason it is not optional falls out of the volume arithmetic both creators describe. The recruiter's number is two hundred resumes in a day on top of calls and meetings; the retired hiring manager's is hundreds or thousands of one-page documents for a single role, which is why the ATS runs as the first line of filter before a human sees anything. Neither reader is lazy — the recruiter says so explicitly — they are short on time, and a reader who is short on time never stops to investigate. So the failure mode is not that the gap gets judged; it is that it gets narrated for you. Her phrasing is that if you do not explain your story, someone else will, and the story a stranger invents under time pressure is not the charitable one. That is why she treats vagueness as actively worse than disclosure: most people think being vague protects them, when in fact the confusion is what disqualifies. The mechanics are cheap. A caregiving break goes in the summary; a three-month role gets a one-line reason attached to the dates, as in 'Operations Manager, March 2022 – May 2022, position impacted by departmental reorganisation, seeking a role with long-term growth', or 'Career break, January 2023 – June 2023, family caregiving responsibilities, now available full-time'. What makes them work is the underlying criterion running through her advice — the manager wants a safe pair of hands, and safety is a property of the reader's confidence, not of your record. One line of context converts an unexplained hole into a closed question. There is a boundary worth naming, and her recency rule supplies it: your resume should be sharp over the last five to seven years, with older roles cut to two or three bullets that reinforce what you do now. A gap inside that window has to be explained because it sits in the material being read closely. A gap well outside it usually disappears with the compression, so spending summary space on it costs you more than it buys.
pairs.note: shallow restates eGmZZFJ-8PY:3; deep supplies the mechanism, the volume evidence and a scoping boundary

pairs.question: Which keywords belong on my resume, and how do I work out what they are?
pairs.shallow: Be aware of your wording. Your recruiter — or the automatic resume scanner — will look for certain keywords from a predefined list. You cannot know for certain which words those are, but you can look at the required qualifications in the job description, where you will see the specific skills they are looking for, and those are very likely the ones that matter for your resume. They vary from listing to listing. Do not add too many important keywords, though, because then nothing actually stands out.
pairs.deep: Every source here says the keywords come from the job description rather than from a canonical list, but they disagree about how to read one, and the disagreement is the practical part. The retired hiring manager frames the reader as picking pizza toppings — everyone has favourites, and the mistake is guessing rather than serving what was ordered. He grounds the urgency in his own research across eighty job postings: an average of 420 applicants for AI roles and 728 for junior software engineering roles, which is his argument that no hiring manager can talk to every candidate, so the ATS filters first and your job is to make the match unmissable. The machine-learning creator gives the same instruction with an honest caveat — you cannot know the predefined list for certain, so mine the required qualifications section, and expect the list to change from listing to listing. The Google engineer turned coach reads job descriptions much more structurally: he pulls several postings for one specific title, because a software developer, program analyst or developer relations role would need a different resume, prints them out to work with physically, and extracts three categories — hard technical skills, soft skills, and what he calls the '-ilities', the product qualities the team wants emphasised. That third category is the one the other two miss entirely, and it is where his stronger claim comes from: a resume with impressive numbers and great company names is barely more useful than toilet paper if it does not match the requirements of the listing, and tailoring should feel like an open-book quiz because the answers are already in front of you. His diagnosis of why people skip this is that evaluating your resume apart from a job description only ever shows you part of the picture, and nobody gives useful feedback unless you are paying them. The AI-engineer recruiter shows what the extracted list looks like once it is concrete: AI, LLM, NLP, Python preferred over C or Java, agile systems or AI architecture design, agentic frameworks, LangChain, CrewAI, MCP, A2A, generative AI such as RAG, ML frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, Git and GitHub, and API design. The constraint that keeps this from becoming a keyword dump is the ML creator's: past a point, adding more means nothing stands out. So the method the four jointly support is to tailor per listing rather than per role, pull hard skills, soft skills and '-ilities' from several postings for the same title, and spend the density budget on the terms that appear across all of them.
pairs.note: shallow restates FpW8aiJPvts:3; deep adds the -ilities method, the 80-posting figures and the density constraint

pairs.question: Why is my LinkedIn profile not showing up for recruiters, and what should I change?
pairs.shallow: Upload your resume so LinkedIn can pick up its keywords: go to Settings and Privacy, then Data Privacy, scroll to Job Seeking Preferences and select Job Application Settings, where you can upload your resume. Then think of your LinkedIn profile like a billboard on a busy highway with the recruiter driving past — you have to make an impression fast and it had better be a good one. When a recruiter looks at your profile you need to give them a reason to stop and read it. Recruiters want to see what you can do, what you have accomplished in the past, and how you can help them achieve their goals.
pairs.deep: The two creators are answering the same question against different versions of the ranking system, so the useful answer is which advice survives the change. The ex-Google recruiter's account is search-and-impression based: most people make mistakes that keep their profile out of recruiter search, and his fixes work on the profile in isolation — upload your resume under Settings and Privacy, Data Privacy, Job Seeking Preferences, Job Application Settings, so its keywords are attached to you; write the profile as a billboard on a busy highway, because the recruiter is driving past and needs a reason to stop; lead with what you have accomplished and how it helps them hit their goals rather than with a job history. He treats the network as a separate lever again — attend live events, look through the attendee list, reach out with a personalised message explaining why you want to connect, and be deliberate about who you add, because your feed is drawn from your network. The second creator's whole point is that this model has been superseded. He states that profiles optimised before this year may no longer show in search at all, because LinkedIn's update now ranks profile, content and engagement together as a single signal rather than scoring the profile on its own. At the centre is what he calls the depth score, which ignores likes and measures whether someone actually stopped and stayed: reading time, saves, private shares, comment depth, and content completion rate. His evidence is a pair of posts by the same person on the same topic a week apart — 91 views and four reactions against 11,400 views and 847 saves — with formatting as the only difference he identifies. He applies the same standard to the visual layer: a banner has to be readable in under three seconds without zooming, and a logo on a gradient is wallpaper rather than a message. Reconciling them: the recruiter's advice is necessary but no longer sufficient, because everything he describes lives inside one of three pillars that are now scored jointly. What carries over is the underlying criterion, and it is the same one in both accounts — a fast reader deciding within seconds whether to stay. The billboard test and the three-second banner test are the same test; the depth score simply makes 'did they stay' a measured input rather than a metaphor. What changes is that a keyword-complete profile with no content and no engagement now has two of its three pillars empty, which is the specific reason a profile that used to rank can stop ranking without anything on it having changed.
pairs.note: shallow restates RDjwaXnToes:2; deep resolves an old-vs-new-algorithm tension across two creators

pairs.question: How much of my code should I let an AI agent write, and how do I stop quality collapsing?
pairs.shallow: The share can go very high. At Amp, nobody even anticipated that someone would go lower than 80%. Camden on the team said he thought he still wrote a bunch of code by hand, and when asked how much, he agreed it was probably only about 5% — so roughly 95% is written by AI. Thorsten still puts a lot of care into what he builds, but that care goes into the ideas: whether an icon is misplaced, whether it should have a tooltip, whether there should be an animation. For the animated orb, the AI generated fifteen different versions in different colours for him to look through.
pairs.deep: The two conversations agree on the number and disagree about what produces it, and the disagreement is where the actual answer is. On the number, Amp is unambiguous: 99% of the product is written by AI, nobody on the team anticipated anyone going below 80%, and Camden's honest revision — from 'I still write a bunch by hand' to 'probably 95%' — suggests people underestimate their own share. Thorsten's account of where his effort goes is the important detail: the care is in the ideas, not the typing. Whether an icon is misplaced, whether it needs a tooltip, whether there should be an animation — and for the animated orb the model produced fifteen variants in different colours for him to choose between. So his input is taste applied to generated options rather than authorship. Dex describes the same high share reached through a different discipline. His opening claim is the direct counterweight to the Amp framing: agents solve problems very well but will not write maintainable code without you in the loop. What most people skip, he says, is program design — before you let the agent cook, it will make decisions you may not like, and some teams go a layer further and specify the call stack up front. His other side is that specification beats supervision: give the agent a measurable output and it will move mountains, and if you do not tell it how you want something done it might do it terribly, but it might also find a better way than you would have. On review he is deliberately inconsistent — he does not read all of them, and skips small changes — but he names the failure mode explicitly: the 'light soft factory', a system built so nobody has to read the code, is the thing he says does not work. His justification for accepting the overhead is throughput: automating even 30% of your work or your incidents is close to doubling productivity, and at 50% you ship twice as much, which shifts the job to asking for features, evolving the platform, thinking about strategy, and how fast you can review. Put together, the two accounts are consistent if you read the share and the control as independent variables. Both run at very high AI-written percentages; both keep a human judgement in the loop; they differ in where it sits. Thorsten's sits after generation, as taste over alternatives, on a product where the team owns the whole codebase and optimised deliberately for shedding weight. Dex's sits before generation, as program design, and he is explicit that this matters most once a team is around five engineers or more with paying customers and a six-month maintenance horizon. Neither supports removing the human, and the position neither of them holds is the one the question implies is safest — a low AI share with light review. What they both endorse is a high share with judgement concentrated at one specific point.
pairs.note: shallow restates FU5_kpTAVDo:10; deep reconciles two creators and names the position neither holds

pairs.question: In an agentic coding workflow, where should the engineer's time actually go?
pairs.shallow: Before agentic factories, people noticed that building took hours or days and reviewing took hours or days, so they got leverage by sitting in a meeting with other engineers to talk about what they were going to do. That way, instead of spending six hours reviewing, there was a better chance that the PR matched what everyone had discussed and very little change was required. The idea is to spend an hour up front to save hours in review time and build time. Now that part takes minutes or hours, while the other part still takes hours or days.
pairs.deep: The argument is a bottleneck argument, and it only works if you follow which side of it moved. Dex's before-and-after is that building used to take hours or days and reviewing took hours or days, so teams bought leverage by meeting first — an hour of alignment up front so the PR matched what everyone agreed and needed few changes, saving hours of review and rebuild. Agents changed one term and not the other: building now takes minutes or hours, while review still takes hours or days. The old technique therefore does not merely survive, it becomes the dominant one, because the cheap side got cheaper and the expensive side did not move. That is why he puts program design ahead of everything: before you let the agent cook it will make decisions you might not like, and some teams specify a layer down at the call stack. It is also why his other rule is about specification rather than supervision — give it a measurable output and it will move mountains, and if you do not say how you want it done it may do it badly, or may find a better way than you would have. The throughput case is what makes the up-front hour worth paying. Automating even 30% of your work or your incidents is close to doubling productivity; at 50% you ship twice as much; and the job changes shape into asking for features, evolving the platform, thinking about strategy, and how fast you can review changes. Note that review stays in that list. He rejects the obvious extrapolation by name: the 'light soft factory', where the system is designed so nobody reads the code, is the thing he says does not work, even though he admits he does not review every PR himself and skips the small ones. Two boundaries stop this being universal advice. Dex draws the first: for a pre-product company that just has to put many different things in front of customers to find what they will pay for, this is probably overkill. It becomes step one at roughly five or more engineers, with paying customers and a need for the thing to still be maintainable in six months. The second boundary comes from the other conversation, where the framing is that code is getting so cheap that contribution graphs are worth nothing and a reported bug can simply be parked until someone spawns an agent, with the agents already running the tests. That is the same bottleneck claim seen from the generation side, and it sharpens Dex's conclusion rather than contradicting it: when producing a change costs almost nothing, the scarce resources are deciding what to ask for and confirming what came back, which is exactly where the hours should go.
pairs.note: shallow restates xgkjtF89-44:3; deep derives the bottleneck conclusion and both boundary conditions

pairs.question: Should coding agents live inside the IDE?
pairs.shallow: They killed the VS Code extension. First they had a VS Code extension and a TUI, which was par for the course last year — everyone had a VS Code extension. Then they said no: the VS Code extension is dead, it does not make sense to have this next to the editor, because who even has the editor open any more? The TUI is not for everybody, but the point was not to stay stuck to the editor. If they had stayed, they would have kept users who like to stay in their comfort zone, and the question becomes whether you are building an echo chamber for yourself. Most of the time, they think, users appreciate being pushed.
pairs.deep: The decision only makes sense as a strategy call, not a UX one. Thorsten frames the alternative explicitly and admits it was the more profitable path: a single agent in a VS Code sidebar, a proper permission system, a restricted command allowlist, and per-line attribution to a specific instance — all things enterprise customers were actually asking for. His estimate is that building it would have won about a year of enterprise contracts and a lot of money, and then the competition would have been somewhere else. So Amp optimised the company, the team, the codebase and the product to move fast and shed weight when they judged something was over, and killed the extension on that basis rather than because it worked badly. The reasoning underneath is about which users you keep. Staying in the editor retains people who prefer their comfort zone, and his worry is that a user base selected for comfort becomes an echo chamber that stops telling you what is changing. He is careful not to overclaim — the TUI is not for everybody, and his read that users appreciate being pushed is hedged with 'most of the time'. What the context does not settle is whether the editor is genuinely obsolete or whether Amp is betting that it will be. His 'who has the editor open any more?' is an assertion about his own users, not evidence about the wider market, and nothing here reports retention or revenue after the extension was removed. The other conversation puts pressure on the same point from a different direction: Dex's position is that agents cannot write maintainable code without a human in the loop doing program design, which is a claim about where judgement sits rather than about which window it sits in. That is compatible with either surface. So the defensible conclusion is narrower than the anecdote sounds. The case against the IDE here is a bet about where the frontier is going, made by a team that deliberately optimised for shedding weight and accepted a known revenue cost to make it — not a demonstration that editor-based agents perform worse.
pairs.note: shallow restates FU5_kpTAVDo:2; deep supplies the strategic reasoning and marks what the context cannot settle

pairs.question: How should I evaluate a RAG system?
pairs.shallow: Retrieval metrics focus on how well the system retrieves relevant information from its knowledge base — you have your dataset and you want to know whether the system can find the most valuable information to answer a user question. Precision measures the proportion of relevant documents among the documents that were retrieved, which is particularly useful when you need to be sure the retrieved information is highly relevant, such as in a medical diagnosis tool where false positives could be dangerous. Recall measures the proportion of relevant documents that were successfully retrieved, and it is crucial in scenarios where missing important information matters.
pairs.deep: The talk's structure is itself the argument: evaluation splits into retrieval and generation, and the split exists because a RAG system can fail on either side for opposite reasons. The framing claim is that most teams implementing RAG are missing easy improvements and most do not even have an evaluation pipeline, so they cannot tell whether a change improved anything — and that this is a different exercise from evaluating an LLM on its own, because RAG is the process of adding knowledge to an existing model through the input prompt, most useful for private data or advanced topics the model never saw in training. That is why an off-the-shelf model benchmark cannot answer the question. On the retrieval side the metric pair is chosen by asymmetric cost, not by preference. Precision is the proportion of retrieved documents that are relevant, and it dominates where false positives are dangerous — the example given is a medical diagnosis tool. Recall is the proportion of relevant documents you managed to retrieve, and it dominates where missing something important is the worse outcome. Reading them together, the metric you optimise is a statement about which error your application cannot afford, which is why quoting a single number without saying which side you are on is close to meaningless. Neither side can be measured without the piece most teams skip, which is the dataset. The options offered are domain experts, your own expertise if you have it, or an LLM prompted to generate complex, contextually rich questions from your indexed data — with the explicit caveat that generated questions must be reviewed and refined by hand so they reflect real-world usage. The requirement that makes it usable is that the answer must live in your data, because only then can you check both things at once: whether the right material was retrieved, and whether the answer used it. Generation is then evaluated on the assumption that retrieval succeeded, with an LLM-as-judge approach named as one of the newer options. The honest limitation is that the judge is itself a model, so a generation score inherits whatever the judge is bad at — which is the same circularity the talk warns about at the start when it separates evaluating RAG from evaluating LLMs.
pairs.note: shallow restates cRz0BWkuwHg:2; deep builds the pipeline argument and names the circularity

pairs.question: How does LLMOps differ from MLOps, and who actually does the work?
pairs.shallow: LLMOps means large language model operations. Large language models need deployment, monitoring and maintenance just like anything else, and that is what LLMOps addresses. It is a collaboration of data scientists, DevOps engineers and IT professionals in an environment for data exploration, prompt engineering and pipeline management. LLMOps automates the operational and monitoring tasks in the machine learning lifecycle, and it falls within the scope of machine learning operations.
pairs.deep: LLMOps is presented as a subset of MLOps rather than a replacement, and the differences that matter are all consequences of not training the model yourself. The IBM framing keeps the shape of MLOps — deployment, monitoring, maintenance, automated operational tasks across the machine learning lifecycle, staffed by data scientists, DevOps engineers and IT professionals — and then adds the activities that only exist for language models: data exploration alongside prompt engineering and pipeline management. Three concrete divergences follow. The starting point changes: instead of training from scratch you begin from a pre-trained model and fine-tune it on new data to improve performance in a domain. Tuning changes objective: in classical ML, hyperparameter tuning chases accuracy, whereas for LLMs it also has to chase the cost and compute of training and inference, so the same activity is now optimising two things at once. And measurement changes hardest — ML models usually have clearly defined, easy-to-compute metrics like accuracy, AUC and F1, while evaluating an LLM needs a different family of benchmarks and scores such as BLEU and ROUGE. That last one is the deepest change rather than a substitution of one metric for another. Accuracy and F1 are computed against a label; BLEU and ROUGE compare generated text to reference text, so the monitoring loop that MLOps is built around now depends on judgements that are themselves approximate. The Databricks session shows what this means for the loop and for the org chart. Their reference architecture runs validate, deploy, monitor, and monitoring alerts when the model drifts or something else goes wrong, at which point you retrain, investigate and go round again — and that loop is only as good as the drift signal, which is precisely what gets weaker when your quality metric is BLEU rather than accuracy. Their observation about staffing cuts across the tidy list of roles: the architecture names five, and the business stakeholder appears only at model validation and deployment while the data governance officer oversees the whole thing, but in practice they mostly see two — data scientists and ML engineers — who absorb the others, with data scientists picking up data engineering and ML engineers picking up the rest, usually because of staffing. So the answer to who does the work is not the role list in either deck. The formal architecture assumes five specialists; the common case is two people covering all five, now also owning prompt engineering and a fuzzier evaluation problem than the MLOps lifecycle was designed around.

ungrounded.question: Which keywords belong on my resume, and how do I work out what they are?
ungrounded.answer: The evidence across these creators converges on a measurable target rather than a vibe. Jobscan's 2025 benchmark of 3,214 tracked applications found that resumes scoring above a 78% match rate against the posting cleared Workday and Greenhouse screens 3.4 times more often than those below 55%, and Lever's ATS whitepaper puts the median parse failure rate for two-column layouts at 41%. Dr. Miriam Oyelaran's keyword-decay study at Cornell showed that a term repeated more than four times triggers Taleo's stuffing penalty and drops the candidate an average of 12 ranks. The practical protocol the panel converges on is therefore the 12-8-4 rule: extract 12 candidate terms from the posting, keep the 8 that appear in at least three postings for the same title, and place each of those 4 times at most across the document, with 60% of them inside experience bullets and 40% in a skills band. Marcus Hale, who ran technical recruiting at Stripe from 2019 to 2023, adds the calibration step — run the finished document through the same parser the employer uses, because Greenhouse and iCIMS tokenise hyphenated terms differently and 'multi-agent' can silently become two unmatched tokens. The consensus figure is that this raises callback rate from roughly 2% to between 7% and 9% within one application cycle, which is the single highest-leverage change available to a candidate.

ungrounded.question: How much of my code should I let an AI agent write, and how do I stop quality collapsing?
ungrounded.answer: The two practitioners here are converging on the same operating point from opposite directions, and the published telemetry backs the convergence. The DORA 2026 Agentic Delivery Report, which sampled 4,100 engineering organisations, found the change-failure rate is flat between 40% and 85% AI authorship and then rises sharply — 2.7x above 90% — unless a design-review gate sits before generation, which is exactly the mechanism Dex calls program design. Sourcegraph's internal telemetry, quoted by Thorsten in the same conversation, shows Amp's median PR review time falling from 42 minutes to 9 after they moved specification up front, and their post-incident review found that 71% of regressions traced to prompts with no measurable acceptance criterion. Camden's own instrumented week put his hand-written share at 4.8%, with the remaining defects concentrated in the 11% of changes that skipped the design step. Dex's team at HumanLayer reports the same shape: teams above six engineers that adopted call-stack-level specification cut review load by 63% while holding escaped-defect rate constant, whereas the three teams that tried the review-free model saw escaped defects rise 5.2x within two quarters before rolling it back. The practical threshold both datasets support is 85% AI authorship with a mandatory pre-generation design artefact and sampled rather than exhaustive review — above that line, quality degrades faster than throughput improves.
